investigation.title: Remote Agent Pod Scheduling Failure: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity on Production Kubernetes Cluster
investigation.summary: All three remote-agents checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api with an identical Kubernetes scheduling error: the cluster's 6 nodes could not place the agent pod because only 2 nodes carry the kata.peerpods.io/vm resource and both are fully consumed, while the remaining 4 nodes do not satisfy the pod's node affinity/selector. Because the pod never scheduled, the eval runner never received a VM ID or remote state, so all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) are absent and every contract assertion is unmet.
investigation.rootCause: The production Kubernetes cluster has exhausted its allocatable kata.peerpods.io/vm capacity. Only 2 of 6 nodes expose this resource, and both report "Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm" at scheduling time. No preemption victims exist, so the scheduler cannot free capacity. Every remote-agent pod submitted during this window is stuck Unschedulable, preventing VM provisioning and causing the eval to time out without producing any evidence. This is a production infrastructure capacity constraint, not an eval infrastructure or code defect. No user-traffic or incident signals are present in the packet, so impact is scoped to the observability eval at this time.

possibleCauses: PRIMARY — kata.peerpods.io/vm resource exhaustion on the 2 eligible nodes: existing remote-agent pods or other workloads have consumed all available VM slots, leaving no capacity for new pods. Supported directly by failed-check.message, sibling.remote-agent-state, and sibling.remote-agent-runtime.

SECONDARY — node affinity/selector mismatch on 4 of 6 nodes: the remote-agent pod spec requires a node label or taint that only the 2 kata-capable nodes carry, so the effective scheduling pool is permanently limited to those 2 nodes. This compounds the capacity problem but is a configuration constraint, not a transient fault.

TERTIARY — a burst of concurrent remote-agent provisioning requests (from other users, other evals, or a runaway cleanup failure) may have temporarily saturated the 2 kata nodes before this eval run began. No cleanup or preemption victims were found, suggesting pods from prior runs may not have been released.

LOWER CONFIDENCE — a node-level failure or cordon on one or both kata-capable nodes could reduce effective capacity to zero even if the resource quota appears non-zero. This cannot be confirmed without kubectl node inspection.

This is an eval-observed infrastructure capacity failure localized to the remote-agents VM scheduling layer; no user-traffic or incident signals are present in the supplied evidence.

investigations.title: Remote Agent Pod Scheduling Failure: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity on Production Kubernetes Cluster
investigations.summary: All three remote-agents checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api with an identical Kubernetes scheduling error: the cluster's 6 nodes could not place the agent pod because only 2 nodes carry the kata.peerpods.io/vm resource and both are fully consumed, while the remaining 4 nodes do not satisfy the pod's node affinity/selector. Because the pod never scheduled, the eval runner never received a VM ID or remote state, so all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) are absent and every contract assertion is unmet.
investigations.rootCause: The production Kubernetes cluster has exhausted its allocatable kata.peerpods.io/vm capacity. Only 2 of 6 nodes expose this resource, and both report "Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm" at scheduling time. No preemption victims exist, so the scheduler cannot free capacity. Every remote-agent pod submitted during this window is stuck Unschedulable, preventing VM provisioning and causing the eval to time out without producing any evidence. This is a production infrastructure capacity constraint, not an eval infrastructure or code defect. No user-traffic or incident signals are present in the packet, so impact is scoped to the observability eval at this time.

recommendedVerifierProbes.reason: infra/evals/status/features.json line 383 sets staleAfterMinutes=360 while infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json line 482 sets max=300. Confirming whether this is intentional determines if the contract needs tightening or the registry needs alignment.

whatWouldDisproveThis: If the GitHub Actions workflow run logs show a successful snapshot publish within the last 300 minutes prior to 2026-07-04T10:33:42Z, the staleness would be unexplained by a missed workflow run and would instead point to a deployment or CDN caching issue.

If fetching https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json now returns a snapshotAgeMinutes value <= 300, it would confirm the workflow has since recovered and the failure was transient.

If the snapshotAgeMinutes value in the live JSON is consistently near 360 (the registry staleAfterMinutes), it would support the hypothesis that the workflow runs on a ~6-hour cadence and the contract max of 300 is misconfigured relative to the actual workflow schedule.

If all other snapshot evidence fields (hasLiveSource, hasNonUnknownFeatureData, generatedAtPresent) were also false or missing, it would suggest a more severe snapshot generation failure rather than a simple scheduling delay.
followUpEvals: Add an eval that directly checks the GitHub Actions workflow run recency for the snapshot-publishing workflow, asserting the last successful run completed within the last 240 minutes (providing buffer before the 300-minute contract threshold).

Add an eval that asserts the registry staleAfterMinutes value for published-observability-snapshot is less than or equal to the expected-output contract's snapshotAgeMinutes max, catching threshold misalignment at configuration time.
Add a trend eval that tracks snapshotAgeMinutes over consecutive runs to detect gradual drift toward the threshold before a hard failure occurs.

Consider a separate eval that checks the overall field value inside the snapshot independently of freshness, so a stale snapshot reporting 'major_outage' does not conflate snapshot staleness with a live system status determination.
